Many oral drugs don't always absorb along one neat first-order path.
Some of the dose absorbs quickly, and the rest absorbs more slowly.
For example, a modified-release tablet can release part of the dose
right away while the rest is released at a constant rate.  This is
where we can use *dual* (or *parallel*) absorption processes.

The model for that is easy to write: two depots, each with its own
absorption, both feeding the central compartment.  The awkward part has
always been the **dose**.  One dose has to end up in two compartments.

## How this is usually done

In NONMEM, the usual approach is to put the dose in the data
**twice**: one record with `CMT=1` and an identical one with `CMT=2`.
The model then sets `F1 = FR` and `F2 = 1 - FR` so each copy carries
its share.  This works, but the dataset no longer describes what was
given and requires you to rewrite the dataset every time you want to
try a new absorption model.  (This is true about compartment numbers
too, this is why `nlmixr2` and `rxode2` can use named compartments)

Monolix avoids the duplication with its PK macros: you write two
`absorption()` macros against the same `adm` and give each a share `p`
(and, if needed, its own `Tlag` or `Tk0`).  The
data keeps one row per dose, and the model decides where the dose goes.

`rxode2` and `nlmixr2` now work the same way.  A **splitting directive** in the
`model({})` block tells `rxode2` to take each dose recorded against one
compartment and send a copy to each of several others.  The dataset keeps
one row per dose, exactly as it was given.  Since `nlmixr2` estimates with
`rxode2` models, the same directive works when you fit.

Everything below works with the current CRAN releases (`rxode2` 5.1.8 and
`nlmixr2est` 7.2.1).

## The four directives

| directive | bolus records become | infusion records become |
|---|---|---|
| `splitBolus(src, a, b, ...)` | a bolus in each target | left alone |
| `splitInfusion(src, a, b, ...)` | left alone | an infusion in each target |
| `splitInfusionBolus(src, a, b, ...)` | an infusion in `a` (the first target), a bolus in the others | an infusion in each target |
| `splitBolusInfusion(src, a, b, ...)` | a bolus in each target except the last, an infusion in the last | an infusion in each target |

The same rules apply to all four:

- **Every target receives the full amount.**  The directive copies the
  dose; it doesn't divide it.  Without any `f()`, each target gets the
  whole dose.  To divide it, give each target a share with `f()`, for
  example `f(depot) <- fr` and `f(slowdepot) <- 1 - fr`.  If you want the
  shares to add up to one, write them that way.

- **Only one splitting directive is allowed per model.**

- **The source can be one of the targets.**  `splitBolus(depot, depot,
  slowdepot)` keeps part of the dose in `depot` and sends a copy to `slowdepot`.
  This is usually what you want: the data says `depot`, and `depot` is
  still one of the absorption routes.  If you leave the source out of the
  target list, the dose doesn't go there at all.  The source is then only a
  label for the data, but it still needs an ODE (`d/dt(sc) <- 0` is
  enough).  The targets themselves must not repeat.

- **You can split into as many compartments as you need.**
  `splitBolus(depot, depot, mid, slowdepot)` gives the full amount to
  3 compartments (`depot`, `mid` and `slowdepot`) and with an `f()` on
  each compartment you could share that amount in any way you want
  with that one dose record.

- **One target moves the dose instead of splitting it.**
  `splitBolus(depot, slowdepot)` sends every bolus recorded against `depot`
  to `slowdepot`, and `depot` gets nothing, even if it has its own ODE.
  `splitInfusion(depot, slowdepot)` does the same for infusions.  This
  is useful when the data says `CMT = depot` but the model wants the dose
  somewhere else, such as the start of a transit chain.  No `f()` is
  needed: the target gets the full dose.

- **A dose type the directive doesn't handle goes to the source
  unchanged.**  Under `splitBolus()`, an infusion recorded against `depot`
  goes into `depot` only and is not split.  If the source isn't a target
  (`d/dt(sc) <- 0`), it is never absorbed at all.  If your data mixes
  boluses and infusions on the source, use one of the two mixed
  directives.

- `alag()`, `f()`, `rate()` and `dur()` on each **target** apply as usual.
  This means each route can have its own lag time.

## Two first-order routes: `splitBolus()`

Here is the classic case: 60% of the dose absorbs quickly and 40% slowly.
The dose stays in `depot` for the fast route, and a copy goes to `slowdepot`
for the slow one:

```{r dual-model}
dual <- function() {
  ini({
    tka1 <- log(1.5);  label("Fast absorption rate ka1 (1/h)")
    tka2 <- log(0.15); label("Slow absorption rate ka2 (1/h)")
    tfr  <- logit(0.6); label("Fraction absorbed by the fast route")
    tcl  <- log(4);    label("Clearance CL (L/h)")
    tv   <- log(40);   label("Volume V (L)")
    eta.ka1 ~ 0.1
    eta.cl  ~ 0.09
    eta.v   ~ 0.04
    prop.sd <- 0.1
  })
  model({
    ka1 <- exp(tka1 + eta.ka1)
    ka2 <- exp(tka2)
    fr  <- expit(tfr)
    cl  <- exp(tcl + eta.cl)
    v   <- exp(tv + eta.v)

    splitBolus(depot, depot, slowdepot) # one depot dose -> depot + slowdepot
    f(depot)     <- fr
    f(slowdepot) <- 1 - fr

    d/dt(depot)     <- -ka1 * depot       # fast route
    d/dt(slowdepot) <- -ka2 * slowdepot   # slow route
    d/dt(central)   <-  ka1 * depot + ka2 * slowdepot - cl / v * central
    cp <- central / v
    cp ~ prop(prop.sd)
  })
}
```

The event table has **one** dose, recorded against `depot`:

```{r dual-sim}
ev <- et(amt = 100, cmt = "depot") |> et(seq(0, 36, by = 0.25))

typical <- rxSolve(dual |> zeroRe(), ev)

typical |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(time, depot, slowdepot, central) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "compartment", values_to = "amount") |>
  ggplot(aes(time, amount, color = compartment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Amount (mg)",
       title = "One 100 mg dose, split 60/40 into a fast and a slow depot")
```

`depot` starts at 60 mg and empties within a few hours.  `slowdepot` starts
at 40 mg and is still emptying a day later.

To check the result, here is the NONMEM-style approach, with the dose
entered twice and no directive.  The two give the same answer:

```{r dual-check}
twoRecords <- function() {
  ini({
    ka1 <- 1.5
    ka2 <- 0.15
    fr <- 0.6
    cl <- 4
    v <- 40
  })
  model({
    f(depot)     <- fr
    f(slowdepot) <- 1 - fr
    d/dt(depot)     <- -ka1 * depot
    d/dt(slowdepot) <- -ka2 * slowdepot
    d/dt(central)   <-  ka1 * depot + ka2 * slowdepot - cl / v * central
    cp <- central / v
  })
}
evTwice <- et(amt = 100, cmt = "depot") |>
  et(amt = 100, cmt = "slowdepot") |>
  et(seq(0, 36, by = 0.25))

all.equal(typical$cp, rxSolve(twoRecords, evTwice)$cp)
```

## Zero-order plus first-order: `splitInfusionBolus()`

Another common shape is a zero-order input straight into the central
compartment (a constant release) combined with first-order absorption
from the depot.  The
dose record is still a plain oral bolus.  `splitInfusionBolus()` turns the
bolus into a **modeled infusion** for the first target and a bolus for the
others.  The first target must declare `dur()` (or `rate()`) so `rxode2`
knows how long the infusion lasts:

```{r zo-model}
zoFo <- function() {
  ini({
    tk0 <- 4;    label("Zero-order duration (h)")
    fr  <- 0.7;  label("Fraction by the zero-order route")
    ka2 <- 1.2;  label("First-order absorption rate (1/h)")
    lag2 <- 1.5; label("Lag time on the first-order route (h)")
    cl  <- 2
    v   <- 25
  })
  model({
    splitInfusionBolus(depot, central, depot)
    dur(central)  <- tk0          # central gets a 4 h zero-order input
    f(central)    <- fr
    f(depot)      <- 1 - fr
    alag(depot)   <- lag2         # the first-order part starts late

    d/dt(depot)   <- -ka2 * depot
    d/dt(central) <-  ka2 * depot - cl / v * central
    cp <- central / v
  })
}

zo <- rxSolve(zoFo, et(amt = 100, cmt = "depot") |> et(seq(0, 24, by = 0.1)))

ggplot(as.data.frame(zo), aes(time, cp)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(1.5, 4), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Concentration (mg/L)",
       title = "70% zero-order over 4 h, 30% first-order after a 1.5 h lag")
```

You can see the shape change at the lag time and again at the end of the
zero-order input.  `splitBolusInfusion(depot, depot, central)` describes
the same model with the targets listed in the other order: there the
**last** target receives the infusion.  Use whichever reads better to you.

Both directives take any number of targets, but only **one** of them
becomes an infusion, and its position is fixed: the first target for
`splitInfusionBolus()`, the last for `splitBolusInfusion()`.  Every other
target gets a bolus.  `splitBolusInfusion(depot, depot, slowdepot, central)`
gives two first-order routes plus a zero-order input.  A `dur()` on a
target in the middle of the list is ignored, and that target silently
gets a bolus.

Two details to watch.  If the infusion target has no `dur()` or
`rate()`, its copy silently stays a bolus, with no warning.  And a
steady-state bolus record (`ss = 1`) is not turned into an infusion:
it is copied as a bolus to each target, and `rxode2` warns you if the
infusion target declared `dur()` or `rate()`. We will work to change
this in the next release (you can track the issue here:
([rxode2#1668](https://github.com/nlmixr2/rxode2/issues/1668)))

## Infusions in the data: `splitInfusion()`

`splitInfusion()` handles doses that are already infusions in the data,
with a `RATE` or `DUR` column, or infusions from a modeled `rate()`/`dur()`.
Each target gets its own copy of the infusion, and `rxode2` moves the start
and the stop records together so they still match.  A subcutaneous
infusion that drains through two pathways looks like this.  This time the
source, `sc`, is **not** a target: it is only the label in the data, so
the whole infusion goes to `fast` and `slow`:

```{r sc-model}
sc <- function() {
  ini({fr <- 0.6; ka1 <- 0.8; ka2 <- 0.05; cl <- 0.2; v <- 3})
  model({
    splitInfusion(sc, fast, slow)
    f(fast) <- fr
    f(slow) <- 1 - fr
    d/dt(sc)      <- 0
    d/dt(fast)    <- -ka1 * fast
    d/dt(slow)    <- -ka2 * slow
    d/dt(central) <-  ka1 * fast + ka2 * slow - cl / v * central
    cp <- central / v
  })
}
```

Remember that `f()` scales the **amount**.  When you scale the amount of
an infusion, `rxode2` follows NONMEM: it holds fixed whichever of rate or
duration the record gives.

If the record gives a `rate`, each copy keeps that rate and runs for a
shorter time.  If the record gives a `dur`, each copy keeps that duration
and runs at a lower rate.  The same 300 mg over 3 hours gives different
profiles depending on how you write it:

```{r sc-rate-dur}
byRate <- rxSolve(sc, et(amt = 300, rate = 100, cmt = "sc") |> et(seq(0, 24, by = 0.1)))
byDur  <- rxSolve(sc, et(amt = 300, dur = 3,    cmt = "sc") |> et(seq(0, 24, by = 0.1)))

bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(byRate) |> mutate(record = "rate = 100 mg/h (copies run 1.8 h and 1.2 h)"),
  as.data.frame(byDur)  |> mutate(record = "dur = 3 h (copies run at 60 and 40 mg/h)")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, cp, color = record)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Concentration (mg/L)", color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Neither is wrong, but you need to know which one your data means.  For a
physical infusion pump that ran for 3 hours, `dur` is probably what you
want.

## Estimation with nlmixr2

The directive is part of the model, so `nlmixr2` uses it with every
estimation method.  The dataset stays the way the clinic recorded it:
one dose row per dose, with `CMT = depot`.

First, simulate 60 subjects who each take 100 mg daily for three days,
with a rich profile after the first and the last dose:

```{r est-data}
set.seed(2026)
rxSetSeed(2026)
nsub <- 60
sampleTimes <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24,
                 48.5, 49, 50, 52, 54, 56, 60, 64, 72)

evPop <- et(amt = 100, cmt = "depot", ii = 24, addl = 2) |>
  et(sampleTimes) |>
  et(id = seq_len(nsub))

sim <- rxSolve(dual, evPop)

doses <- data.frame(ID = seq_len(nsub), TIME = 0, EVID = 1, AMT = 100,
                    II = 24, ADDL = 2, CMT = "depot", DV = NA)

obs <- as.data.frame(sim) |>
  transmute(ID = id, TIME = time, EVID = 0, AMT = 0, II = 0, ADDL = 0,
            CMT = "cp", DV = sim)

dat <- bind_rows(doses, obs) |> arrange(ID, TIME, desc(EVID))

head(dat, 4)
```

Notice that the dataset never mentions `slowdepot`.  The
absorption model is in the model, and only there.

The example builds the dose rows directly rather than taking them from
`rxSolve(..., addDosing = TRUE)`.  When a model splits its doses, the dose
rows that `addDosing` returns are the **translated** records, one for
`depot` and one for `slowdepot`.  The output then has two dose rows per dose,
which is the NONMEM-style data this approach is meant to avoid.

Now fit it with FOCEi and with SAEM.  It's the same model function and
the same data:

```{r est-fit, results = "hide"}
fitF := nlmixr(dual, dat, "focei", control = foceiControl(print = 0))
fitS := nlmixr(dual, dat, "saem",  control = saemControl(print = 0))
```

```{r est-table}
truth <- c(tka1 = 1.5, tka2 = 0.15, tfr = 0.6, tcl = 4, tv = 40)

est <- function(fit, method) {
  fit$parFixedDf[names(truth), ] |>
    mutate(parameter = names(truth),
           !!method := sprintf("%.3g", `Back-transformed`)) |>
    select(parameter, all_of(method))
}

data.frame(parameter = names(truth),
           label = c("ka1 (1/h)", "ka2 (1/h)", "fast fraction",
                     "CL (L/h)", "V (L)"),
           truth = sprintf("%.3g", truth)) |>
  left_join(est(fitF, "FOCEi"), by = "parameter") |>
  left_join(est(fitS, "SAEM"),  by = "parameter") |>
  select(-parameter) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

Both methods come back close to the values that generated the data.  The
fraction absorbed by the fast route is often the hardest parameter to
estimate in a dual-absorption model, and both methods land within a few
percent of it.

Everything you do after the fit uses the same model, so the split keeps
working.  A VPC simulates from the fitted model with the original
one-row-per-dose data.  The bins are set by hand, halfway between the
nominal sample times, so that the 24 h troughs aren't binned with the
samples after the last dose:

```{r est-vpc, fig.height = 4.2}
times <- c(0, sampleTimes)
bins  <- c(0, (head(times, -1) + tail(times, -1)) / 2, 80)
vpcPlot(fitS, n = 300, bins = bins, show = list(obs_dv = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Concentration (mg/L)",
       title = "VPC of the SAEM fit")
```

The same applies to `augPred()`, `rxSolve(fit, newEvents)` for a new
regimen, and the other post-fit tools: you give them one row per dose.

## Doses added while solving

The [adaptive dosing post](https://blog.nlmixr2.org/blog/2026-09-09-adaptive-dosing/) showed how a
model can add doses during the solve with `bolus()` and the other `evid_()`
helpers.  `splitBolus()` applies to those doses too.  A rescue dose that
the model adds to `depot` is split between `depot` and `slowdepot`, just
like a dose from the data:

```{r adaptive}
rescue <- function() {
  ini({ka1 <- 1.5; ka2 <- 0.15; fr <- 0.6; cl <- 4; v <- 40})
  model({
    splitBolus(depot, depot, slowdepot)
    f(depot)     <- fr
    f(slowdepot) <- 1 - fr
    d/dt(depot)     <- -ka1 * depot
    d/dt(slowdepot) <- -ka2 * slowdepot
    d/dt(central)   <-  ka1 * depot + ka2 * slowdepot - cl / v * central
    cp <- central / v
    # every 24 h, top up if the trough is below 0.5 mg/L
    if (t > 0 && t %% 24 == 0 && cp < 0.5) {
      bolus(100)
    }
  })
}
resc <- rxSolve(rescue, et(amt = 100, cmt = "depot") |> et(seq(0, 96, by = 0.05)))

resc |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(time, depot, slowdepot) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "compartment", values_to = "amount") |>
  ggplot(aes(time, amount, color = compartment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Amount (mg)",
       title = "Doses the model adds are split 60/40 too")
```

The other three directives work at data-translation time only.  Doses
added during the solve are **not** split by `splitInfusion()`,
`splitInfusionBolus()` or `splitBolusInfusion()`.  If an adaptive model
needs to add doses to a split route, use `splitBolus()`.

## Summary

- Put **one** dose row per dose in the data, recorded against a source
  compartment (`depot`, `sc`, ...).  The source can also be one of the
  targets.
- Add a splitting directive to `model({})` to say where that dose goes:
  `splitBolus()`, `splitInfusion()`, `splitInfusionBolus()` or
  `splitBolusInfusion()`.
- Use `f()` to give each target its share, and `alag()`, `dur()` or
  `rate()` to give each route its own timing.
- The same model simulates in `rxode2` and fits in `nlmixr2` (FOCEi,
  SAEM and the rest), and the post-fit tools apply the split too.

More detail, including the edge cases, is in `?splitBolus`,
`?splitInfusion`, `` ?`splitInfusionBolus-directive` `` and
`` ?`splitBolusInfusion-directive` ``.

```{r featured, include = FALSE}
p <- typical |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(time, depot, slowdepot, central) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "compartment", values_to = "amount") |>
  ggplot(aes(time, amount, color = compartment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  labs(x = "Time (h)", y = "Amount (mg)", color = NULL,
       title = "One dose record, two absorption routes") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
ggsave("featured.png", p, width = 8, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
```
